claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction is associated with activation of the integrated stress response (ISR).
source: Mitochondrial dysfunction is associated with activation of the integrated stress response (ISR) but the underlying triggers remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known association, supported by citations throughout the introduction.

claim: In myoblasts, impaired NADH oxidation upon electron transport chain (ETC) inhibition depletes asparagine.
source: In myoblasts, we find that impaired NADH oxidation upon electron transport chain (ETC) inhibition depletes asparagine, activating the ISR via the eIF2α kinase GCN2.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Asparagine depletion in myoblasts activates the ISR via the eIF2α kinase GCN2.
source: In myoblasts, we find that impaired NADH oxidation upon electron transport chain (ETC) inhibition depletes asparagine, activating the ISR via the eIF2α kinase GCN2.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4K-M.

claim: In myotubes, impaired NADH oxidation following ETC inhibition neither depletes asparagine nor activates the ISR.
source: In myotubes, however, impaired NADH oxidation following ETC inhibition neither depletes asparagine nor activates the ISR, reflecting an altered metabolic state.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: ATP synthase inhibition in myotubes triggers the ISR via a mechanism related to mitochondrial inner-membrane hyperpolarization.
source: ATP synthase inhibition in myotubes triggers the ISR via a distinct mechanism related to mitochondrial inner-membrane hyperpolarization.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5I.

claim: There is no universal mechanism linking mitochondrial dysfunction to ISR activation.
source: Our work dispels the notion of a universal path linking mitochondrial dysfunction to the ISR, instead revealing multiple paths that depend both on the nature of the mitochondrial defect and on the metabolic state of the cell.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by the contrasting results in myoblasts versus myotubes.

claim: The ETC provides the driving force for ATP synthesis by oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).
source: It provides the driving force for ATP synthesis by oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) (Mitchell, 1961; Mitchell, 2011)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Mitchell's work.

claim: The ETC maintains redox balance of cofactor pairs (NADH:NAD+, CoQH2:CoQ) that are coupled to hundreds of cellular reactions.
source: maintains redox balance of cofactor pairs (NADH:NAD+, CoQH2:CoQ) that are coupled to hundreds of cellular reactions (Williamson et al., 1967; Ying, 2008; Santidrian et al., 2013; Titov et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2018; Goodman et al., 2018; Mitchell, 1975; Turunen et al., 2004; Alcázar-Fabra et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Mutations in nearly 300 nuclear or mitochondrial (mtDNA) genes have been implicated in mitochondrial disorders.
source: Mutations in nearly 300 nuclear or mitochondrial (mtDNA) genes have been implicated in mitochondrial disorders that affect at least 1 in 4300 live births and lack effective treatments (Schapira, 2012; Vafai and Mootha, 2012; Gorman et al., 2015; Gorman et al., 2016; Frazier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Mitochondrial disorders affect at least 1 in 4300 live births.
source: Mutations in nearly 300 nuclear or mitochondrial (mtDNA) genes have been implicated in mitochondrial disorders that affect at least 1 in 4300 live births and lack effective treatments (Schapira, 2012; Vafai and Mootha, 2012; Gorman et al., 2015; Gorman et al., 2016; Frazier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Mitochondrial disorders lack effective treatments.
source: Mutations in nearly 300 nuclear or mitochondrial (mtDNA) genes have been implicated in mitochondrial disorders that affect at least 1 in 4300 live births and lack effective treatments (Schapira, 2012; Vafai and Mootha, 2012; Gorman et al., 2015; Gorman et al., 2016; Frazier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Studies in patients, animals and cultured cells have consistently identified a gene expression program associated with the integrated stress response (ISR) as a signature of mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Studies in patients, animals and cultured cells have consistently identified a gene expression program associated with the integrated stress response (ISR) as a signature of mitochondrial dysfunction (Martinus et al., 1996; Zhao et al., 2002; Kühl et al., 2017; Celardo et al., 2017; Quirós et al., 2017; Fujita et al., 2007; Silva et al., 2009; Tyynismaa et al., 2010; Dogan et al., 2014; Bao et al., 2016; Magarin et al., 2016; Lehtonen et al., 2016; Khan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with extensive supporting citations.

claim: The ISR is triggered by various insults, including nutrient deficiency, unfolded protein stress and pathogen infection.
source: The ISR is triggered by various insults, including nutrient deficiency, unfolded protein stress and pathogen infection.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the ISR.

claim: In mammalian cells, the ISR is typically activated by a family of four kinases that phosphorylate eIF2α.
source: In mammalian cells, it is typically activated by a family of four kinases, each of which can phosphorylate the alpha subunit of translation initiation factor 2 (eIF2α) in response to distinct stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the ISR mechanism.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation acutely inhibits global protein synthesis.
source: eIF2α phosphorylation acutely inhibits global protein synthesis but promotes translation of transcription factors, such as activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) and DNA damage-inducible transcript three protein (DDIT3), that then engage their downstream targets (Harding et al., 2003; Palam et al., 2011; Harding et al., 2000; Vattem and Wek, 2004; Wek, 2018; Pakos‐Zebrucka et al., 2016; Taniuchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation promotes translation of transcription factors ATF4 and DDIT3.
source: eIF2α phosphorylation acutely inhibits global protein synthesis but promotes translation of transcription factors, such as activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) and DNA damage-inducible transcript three protein (DDIT3), that then engage their downstream targets (Harding et al., 2003; Palam et al., 2011; Harding et al., 2000; Vattem and Wek, 2004; Wek, 2018; Pakos‐Zebrucka et al., 2016; Taniuchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The ISR activates the mitochondrial 1-carbon pathway in tissues affected by mitochondrial disease.
source: In tissues affected by mitochondrial disease, the ISR activates the mitochondrial 1-carbon pathway (Kühl et al., 2017; Tyynismaa et al., 2010; Bao et al., 2016; Nikkanen et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The ISR is thought to underlie secretion of the circulating cytokines FGF21 and GDF15 that are under consideration as disease biomarkers.
source: and is thought to underlie secretion of the circulating cytokines fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) and growth/differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) that are under consideration as disease biomarkers (Lehtonen et al., 2016; Fujita et al., 2015; Yatsuga et al., 2015; Chung et al., 2017; Miyake et al., 2016; Restelli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations and uses 'thought to' indicating inference from literature.

claim: It remains unclear whether the ISR plays a protective role in mitochondrial disease or contributes to pathology.
source: It remains unclear whether the ISR plays a protective role in mitochondrial disease or rather contributes to pathology (Khan et al., 2017; Suomalainen and Battersby, 2018; Lamech and Haynes, 2015).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as an open question with supporting citations.

claim: Defects in mtDNA maintenance and expression are most frequently associated with ISR activation in vivo.
source: Defects in mtDNA maintenance and expression are most frequently associated with ISR activation in vivo (Kühl et al., 2017; Lehtonen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: C2C12 mouse myoblasts can be induced to exit the cell cycle and terminally differentiate into myotubes.
source: To this end, we utilized proliferating C2C12 mouse myoblasts, which can be induced to exit the cell cycle and then terminally differentiate into myotubes (Yaffe and Saxel, 1977; Blau et al., 1985; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Differentiation triggers mitochondrial biogenesis in C2C12 cells.
source: Differentiation triggers mitochondrial biogenesis and promotes oxidative metabolism as the cells shift from a primary focus on nutrient uptake and biosynthesis to self-maintenance and specialized functions (Moyes et al., 1997; Leary et al., 1998; Casadei et al., 2009; Remels et al., 2010; Sin et al., 2016; Vander Heiden et al., 2009; Lemons et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Differentiation promotes oxidative metabolism in C2C12 cells.
source: Differentiation triggers mitochondrial biogenesis and promotes oxidative metabolism as the cells shift from a primary focus on nutrient uptake and biosynthesis to self-maintenance and specialized functions (Moyes et al., 1997; Leary et al., 1998; Casadei et al., 2009; Remels et al., 2010; Sin et al., 2016; Vander Heiden et al., 2009; Lemons et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Complex I or complex III inhibition abrogated mitochondrial oxygen consumption.
source: Complex I or complex III inhibition abrogated mitochondrial oxygen consumption while cells treated with the ATP synthase inhibitor retained residual respiration, not coupled to ATP synthesis, often termed oligomycin-resistant respiration or leak respiration (Jastroch et al., 2010; Divakaruni and Brand, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cells treated with ATP synthase inhibitor retained residual respiration not coupled to ATP synthesis.
source: Complex I or complex III inhibition abrogated mitochondrial oxygen consumption while cells treated with the ATP synthase inhibitor retained residual respiration, not coupled to ATP synthesis, often termed oligomycin-resistant respiration or leak respiration (Jastroch et al., 2010; Divakaruni and Brand, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Myotube mitochondria showed less leak respiration than myoblasts, indicative of tighter coupling.
source: Myotube mitochondria showed less leak respiration, indicative of tighter coupling (Sin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and can be inferred from Figure 1C.

claim: PCA of gene expression revealed a dominant first principal component (PC1; 57% of the variance) along which inhibited myoblasts progressed.
source: PCA of myoblast gene expression revealed a dominant first principal component (PC1; 57% of the variance) along which inhibited cells progressed, with piericidin and antimycin exerting a more pronounced effect than oligomycin (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Piericidin and antimycin exerted a more pronounced effect than oligomycin on PC1 in myoblasts.
source: PCA of myoblast gene expression revealed a dominant first principal component (PC1; 57% of the variance) along which inhibited cells progressed, with piericidin and antimycin exerting a more pronounced effect than oligomycin (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cis-regulatory analysis identified binding motifs for ATF4 as the most enriched in promoters of genes upregulated along PC1 in myoblasts.
source: Cis-regulatory analysis identified binding motifs for the ISR master regulator ATF4 as the most enriched in promoters of genes upregulated along PC1 (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GSEA highlighted pathways typically upregulated as part of the ISR in myoblasts treated with inhibitors.
source: while GSEA highlighted pathways typically upregulated as part of the ISR, including cytosolic tRNA synthetases and translation factors, amino acid transport and biosynthesis genes, and additional ISR regulators (Harding et al., 2003; Han et al., 2013; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Promoters of downregulated genes in myoblasts were enriched for motifs of E2F-family transcription factors.
source: Promoters of downregulated genes were enriched for motifs or ChIP-seq peaks of E2F-family transcription factors, master regulators of the cell cycle (Johnson et al., 1993; Helin, 1998; Ren et al., 2002; Fischer and Müller, 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Promoters of downregulated genes in myoblasts were enriched for motifs of SREBP-1/2.
source: and of SREBP-1/2, regulators of cholesterol and lipid metabolism (Yokoyama et al., 1993; Hua et al., 1993; Wang et al., 1994; Horton et al., 2002; Figure 2B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The cell cycle, DNA replication and cholesterol biosynthesis pathways were the most sharply depressed in myoblasts treated with inhibitors.
source: The cell cycle, DNA replication and cholesterol biosynthesis pathways also emerged as the most sharply depressed in the GSEA results (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Inhibitor treatments in myoblasts were accompanied by eIF2α phosphorylation and ATF4 protein accumulation.
source: Nevertheless, the transcriptional signatures we observed were accompanied in all cases by eIF2α phosphorylation and ATF4 protein accumulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Complex I or complex III inhibition triggered the ISR more potently than ATP synthase inhibition in myoblasts.
source: In myoblasts, complex I or complex III inhibition triggered the ISR more potently than ATP synthase inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Complex I or complex III inhibition elevated whole-cell NADH/NAD+ more than ATP synthase inhibition in myoblasts.
source: We confirmed that complex I or complex III inhibition elevated whole-cell NADH/NAD+, which primarily reflects the mitochondrial ratio (Titov et al., 2016; Sies, 1982; Eng et al., 1989), more so than ATP synthase inhibition (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The increase in whole-cell NADH/NAD+ was prevented by mitoLbNOX in myoblasts.
source: The increase in whole-cell NADH/NAD+ was prevented in all cases by mitoLbNOX, as expected
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LbNOX expression was sufficient to almost completely ablate ISR activation upon complex I or complex III inhibition in myoblasts.
source: Strikingly, LbNOX expression was sufficient to almost completely ablate ISR activation, represented by the Ddit3 transcript, upon complex I or complex III inhibition but only partially mitigated ISR activation by ATP synthase inhibition (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: mitoLbNOX significantly attenuated ISR activation during complex I inhibition in myoblasts.
source: mitoLbNOX also significantly attenuated ISR activation during complex I inhibition but proved less effective during complex III inhibition, possibly due to its failure to fully oxidize the cytosol in this case.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Impaired NADH oxidation was the primary trigger of ISR-related gene expression in myoblasts.
source: Thus, impaired NADH oxidation was the primary trigger of ISR-related gene expression in myoblasts and correcting the NADH imbalance in the cytosol was sufficient to prevent this
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data in Figure 3F.

claim: Correcting the NADH imbalance in the cytosol was sufficient to prevent ISR-related gene expression in myoblasts.
source: Thus, impaired NADH oxidation was the primary trigger of ISR-related gene expression in myoblasts and correcting the NADH imbalance in the cytosol was sufficient to prevent this
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data in Figure 3F.

claim: Complex III dysfunction activates p53 due to a pyrimidine deficiency that results from inability of DHODH to donate electrons to CoQ.
source: Complex III dysfunction has been shown to activate p53 due to a pyrimidine deficiency that results from inability of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) to donate electrons to CoQ (Khutornenko et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: p53 activation downregulated Atf4 and shut down ISR gene expression following complex III inhibition.
source: p53 activation downregulated Atf4 in this setting and shut down ISR gene expression (Evstafieva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: p53 activation following complex III inhibition was dependent on an oxidized cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratio.
source: Thus, p53 activation following complex III inhibition was dependent on an oxidized cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratio and required to fully ablate the ISR.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data in Figure 3H.

claim: LbNOX modestly stimulated glycolysis during complex I inhibition in myoblasts.
source: Using lactate secretion as a proxy for glycolytic flux, we found that LbNOX did modestly stimulate glycolysis (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: LbNOX did not improve adenylate energy charge during complex I inhibition in myoblasts.
source: However, this did not translate into an improved energy charge, and in fact, the opposite was true (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Aspartate and asparagine emerged among the top metabolites depleted by piericidin in a manner responsive to oxidizing the cytosol in myoblasts.
source: The amino acids aspartate and its derivative asparagine, alongside related TCA cycle intermediates, emerged among the top metabolites depleted by piericidin in a manner responsive to oxidizing the cytosol.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Piericidin treatment caused a ~16 fold drop in aspartate within 1 hr in control myoblasts.
source: Absolute quantification confirmed a ~ 16 fold drop in aspartate within 1 hr of piericidin treatment in control cells compared with only a 2.5-fold drop in LbNOX cells (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Piericidin treatment caused only a 2.5-fold drop in aspartate in LbNOX myoblasts.
source: Absolute quantification confirmed a ~ 16 fold drop in aspartate within 1 hr of piericidin treatment in control cells compared with only a 2.5-fold drop in LbNOX cells (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Amino acid deficiency is a canonical ISR trigger through the eIF2α kinase GCN2.
source: Amino acid deficiency is a canonical ISR trigger through the eIF2α kinase GCN2, which is activated due to uncharged tRNA (Hinnebusch, 1984; Dever et al., 1992; Wek et al., 1995; Berlanga et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2002; Castilho et al., 2014; Inglis et al., 2019; Harding et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: 10 mM aspartate significantly attenuated ISR activation upon complex I inhibition in myoblasts.
source: Indeed, 10 mM aspartate significantly attenuated ISR activation upon complex I inhibition, though not to the same extent as LbNOX (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Aspartate addition did not indirectly oxidize cytosolic NADH/NAD+ during complex I inhibition in myoblasts.
source: Importantly, aspartate addition did not indirectly oxidize cytosolic NADH/NAD+ (Figure 4G)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Aspartate was insufficient to appreciably restore cell proliferation during complex I inhibition in myoblasts.
source: and was insufficient to appreciably restore cell proliferation (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: GCN2iB significantly suppressed ISR gene expression in response to complex I inhibition in myoblasts.
source: Indeed, co-treatment with GCN2iB significantly suppressed ISR gene expression in response to complex I inhibition but had no effect on ISR activation in response to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress induced by tunicamycin (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4K.

claim: GCN2iB had no effect on ISR activation in response to ER stress induced by tunicamycin in myoblasts.
source: Indeed, co-treatment with GCN2iB significantly suppressed ISR gene expression in response to complex I inhibition but had no effect on ISR activation in response to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress induced by tunicamycin (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4K.

claim: 6 hr of complex I inhibition resulted in marked GCN2 activation in myoblasts.
source: Using autophosphorylation at Threonine-898 as a readout of kinase activation (Romano et al., 1998), we observed that 6 hr of complex I inhibition resulted in marked GCN2 activation, which was partially attenuated by supplementing aspartate (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Asparagine alone abrogated GCN2 activation during complex I inhibition in myoblasts.
source: Strikingly, asparagine alone abrogated GCN2 activation with no discernible additive effect of aspartate, suggesting the drop in asparagine was the most proximal activating signal.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4L.

claim: LbNOX expression effectively prevented GCN2 activation during complex I inhibition in myoblasts.
source: As expected, LbNOX expression, which enables synthesis of both amino acids during complex I inhibition, effectively prevented GCN2 activation
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4L.

claim: GCN2 was required to attain the threshold eIF2α phosphorylation level that elicits ATF4 translation in myoblasts.
source: GCN2iB completely prevented ATF4 protein accumulation despite some residual eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 4L), suggesting GCN2 was required to attain the threshold phosphorylation level that elicits ATF4 translation.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the data in Figure 4L.

claim: In myoblasts, the rise in the NADH/NAD+ ratio is a major driver of ISR-related gene expression following complex I inhibition.
source: Collectively, these experiments indicate that in myoblasts, the rise in the NADH/NAD+ ratio is a major driver of ISR-related gene expression following complex I inhibition, as it limits biosynthesis of aspartate, depletes asparagine and activates GCN2 (Figure 4N).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Myotubes only experienced significant gene expression changes upon ATP synthase inhibition.
source: In contrast to myoblasts, myotubes only experienced significant gene expression changes upon ATP synthase inhibition (PC1; 50% of the variance) (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Gene expression changes in myotubes upon ATP synthase inhibition were driven by ISR activation.
source: In contrast to myoblasts, myotubes only experienced significant gene expression changes upon ATP synthase inhibition (PC1; 50% of the variance) (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 1), driven once more by ISR activation (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: ETC inhibition had little effect on gene expression in myotubes.
source: In contrast to myoblasts, myotubes only experienced significant gene expression changes upon ATP synthase inhibition (PC1; 50% of the variance) (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 1), driven once more by ISR activation (Figure 5B), whereas ETC inhibition had little effect.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The shift in the pattern of ISR activation was evident as soon as 24 hr after the switch to low serum.
source: The shift in the pattern of ISR activation was already evident as soon as 24 hr after the switch to low serum, when cells are largely post-mitotic but far from differentiated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Myotubes experienced a significant increase in both mitochondrial and cytosolic NADH/NAD+ during ETC inhibition.
source: Myotubes did experience a significant increase in both the mitochondrial and the cytosolic ratio during ETC inhibition (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The mitochondrial and cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratios were not tightly linked in myotubes.
source: However, the ratios were not tightly linked, as in myoblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Oxidizing mitochondrial NADH with mitoLbNOX failed to oxidize cytosolic NADH/NAD+ in myotubes.
source: The severity of NADH imbalance across the inhibitors was discordant between the compartments and oxidizing mitochondrial NADH with mitoLbNOX failed to oxidize cytosolic NADH/NAD+.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Myotubes did not rely on complex I to oxidize cytosolic reducing equivalents via the malate-aspartate shuttle.
source: These results suggest myotubes did not rely on complex I to oxidize cytosolic reducing equivalents via the malate-aspartate shuttle.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the data in Figure 5D.

claim: Cytosolic NADH/NAD+ in myotubes likely increased due to activation of glycolysis.
source: Rather, cytosolic NADH/NAD+ likely increased due to activation of glycolysis, evidenced by a ~ 75% rise in lactate secretion (Figure 5E)
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the data in Figure 5E.

claim: Complex I or complex III inhibition caused only a modest decrease in intracellular aspartate in myotubes.
source: Despite elevated mitochondrial and cytosolic NADH/NAD+, complex I or complex III inhibition caused only a modest decrease (2-fold and 4-fold, respectively) in intracellular aspartate whereas ATP synthase inhibition even led to a slight accumulation (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: None of the inhibitor treatments depleted asparagine in myotubes.
source: None of the treatments depleted asparagine, which in fact accumulated (Figure 5H)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The absence of asparagine deficiency likely explains why myotubes do not activate the ISR when complex I or complex III is inhibited.
source: The absence of asparagine deficiency likely explains why myotubes do not activate the ISR when complex I or complex III is inhibited.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the data.

claim: Myotubes failed to trigger the ISR after mitochondrial protein synthesis was blocked for 48 hr.
source: Myotubes also failed to trigger the ISR after mitochondrial protein synthesis was blocked for 48 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only ATP synthase inhibition is associated with inner-membrane hyperpolarization.
source: Inhibition of complex I, complex III or ATP synthase all acutely impair NADH oxidation and OXPHOS but their effects on mitochondrial membrane potential are distinct. Only ATP synthase inhibition is associated with inner-membrane hyperpolarization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Treating myotubes with oligomycin in combination with piericidin significantly attenuated the ISR.
source: All three interventions significantly attenuated the ISR (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Treating myotubes with oligomycin after pre-conditioning in mild hypoxia significantly attenuated the ISR.
source: All three interventions significantly attenuated the ISR (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Treating myotubes with oligomycin in combination with a mild dose of BAM15 significantly attenuated the ISR.
source: All three interventions significantly attenuated the ISR (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: LbNOX expression did not attenuate the ISR in oligomycin-treated myotubes.
source: whereas LbNOX expression did not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Hyperpolarization is the key factor in the signal relay linking ATP synthase inhibition to ISR activation in myotubes.
source: implicating hyperpolarization as the key factor in the signal relay (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data in Figure 5I.

claim: A higher dose of BAM15 triggered the ISR on its own in myotubes.
source: Intriguingly, a higher dose of BAM15 triggered the ISR on its own, suggesting perturbation to membrane potential in either direction was sensed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Aspartate is largely produced from TCA cycle-derived oxaloacetate (OAA).
source: Aspartate is largely produced from TCA cycle-derived oxaloacetate (OAA) but elevated mitochondrial NADH/NAD+ blocks the oxidative TCA cycle when complex I is inhibited (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Elevated mitochondrial NADH/NAD+ blocks the oxidative TCA cycle when complex I is inhibited.
source: Aspartate is largely produced from TCA cycle-derived oxaloacetate (OAA) but elevated mitochondrial NADH/NAD+ blocks the oxidative TCA cycle when complex I is inhibited (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The cytosolic aspartate and asparagine biosynthesis enzymes are both ISR targets.
source: The cytosolic aspartate and asparagine biosynthesis enzymes are both ISR targets (Fujita et al., 2007; Harding et al., 2003; Han et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Asparagine cannot be converted to aspartate in most mammalian cells.
source: Supplementation with asparagine alone, which cannot be converted to aspartate in most mammalian cells (Pavlova et al., 2018), was sufficient to abrogate GCN2 activation (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The KM values for aspartate and asparagine of their respective cytosolic tRNA synthetases are similar (~15–30 μM).
source: This result may be explained by the fact that while the KM values for aspartate and asparagine of their respective cytosolic tRNA synthetases are similar (~15–30 μM) (Bour et al., 2009; Messmer et al., 2009; Andrulis et al., 1978)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Cellular aspartate concentration is estimated at ~5–10 mM.
source: Aspartate is estimated at ~5–10 mM whereas asparagine is much closer to the KM, at ~100–200 μM (Chen et al., 2016; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Cellular asparagine concentration is estimated at ~100–200 μM.
source: Aspartate is estimated at ~5–10 mM whereas asparagine is much closer to the KM, at ~100–200 μM (Chen et al., 2016; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The KM for aspartate of asparagine synthetase is much higher (~1 mM) than the KM of aspartyl-tRNA synthetase.
source: The KM for aspartate of asparagine synthetase is much higher (~1 mM) (Horowitz and Meister, 1972; Ciustea et al., 2005), so aspartate deficiency readily depletes asparagine (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Asparagine tRNA charging is a sensitive sensor of NADH reductive stress in proliferating cells.
source: We conclude asparagine tRNA charging is a sensitive sensor of NADH reductive stress in proliferating cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental data and reasoning.

claim: The pyrimidine deficiency resulting from an overly-reduced CoQ triggered p53 to shut down ISR gene expression only when cytosolic reductive stress was resolved.
source: Surprisingly, we also found that NADH reductive stress was a key modulator of an interaction between the ISR and p53 during complex III inhibition in myoblasts. The pyrimidine deficiency resulting from an overly-reduced CoQ triggered p53 to shut down ISR gene expression only when cytosolic reductive stress was resolved (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated as a finding based on the data in Figure 3G.

claim: Myoblasts relied on complex I to oxidize cytosolic reducing equivalents via the malate-aspartate shuttle.
source: Moreover, myoblasts relied on complex I to oxidize cytosolic reducing equivalents via the malate-aspartate shuttle whereas this was absent in myotubes (Figure 3D, Figure 5D)
evidence: This is stated as a finding based on the data in Figures 3D and 5D.

claim: The malate-aspartate shuttle was absent in myotubes.
source: Moreover, myoblasts relied on complex I to oxidize cytosolic reducing equivalents via the malate-aspartate shuttle whereas this was absent in myotubes (Figure 3D, Figure 5D), consistent with observations in skeletal muscle in vivo (Sahlin et al., 1987; MacDonald and Marshall, 2000; Alfadda et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a finding based on the data in Figures 3D and 5D, with supporting citations.

claim: In respiring cells, oligomycin typically hyperpolarizes the inner-membrane as it blocks a major consumer of the proton gradient.
source: In respiring cells, oligomycin typically hyperpolarizes the inner-membrane as it blocks a major consumer of the proton gradient (Brand and Nicholls, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The eIF2α kinase HRI potently triggers the ISR in response to either ATP synthase inhibition or severe depolarization.
source: While this paper was in revision, Guo et al. and Fessler et al. reported that the eIF2α kinase HRI potently triggers the ISR in response to either ATP synthase inhibition or severe depolarization (Fessler et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated as recent findings from other studies with supporting citations.

claim: HRI activation depended on processing of the inner-membrane protein DELE1 by the inner-membrane protease OMA1.
source: HRI activation depended on processing of the inner-membrane protein DELE1 by the inner-membrane protease OMA1 (Fessler et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as recent findings from other studies with supporting citations.

claim: OMA1 has been shown to respond to both depolarization and hyperpolarization.
source: It is tempting to speculate this mechanism is operative in our system, as OMA1 has been shown to respond to both depolarization and hyperpolarization (Ehses et al., 2009; Baker et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Pyruvate therapy was recently shown to decrease serum GDF15 in mitochondrial disease patients.
source: We note pyruvate therapy, which serves to regenerate NAD+, was recently shown to decrease serum GDF15, a circulating marker of the ISR, in mitochondrial disease patients (Koga et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding with a supporting citation.

claim: The response to mitochondrial inhibition was not activated simply due to the effects of OXPHOS inhibition on energy metabolism, so long as glucose was available.
source: The response was not activated simply due to the effects of OXPHOS inhibition on energy metabolism, so long as glucose was available.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Blockade of mtDNA-encoded protein synthesis did not appear to be directly monitored in either myoblasts or myotubes.
source: And blockade of mtDNA-encoded protein synthesis did not appear to be directly monitored in either cell state (Figure 3G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data in Figure 3G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.
